timeline_list.title: Challenging a Society
timeline_list.description: In 1940, Hattie McDaniel (1893-1952) wins the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress for Gone with the Wind (1939), becoming the first Black actress in history to win an Oscar. When the film was released, she was barred from attending the premiere; at the awards ceremony, she was not allowed to sit at the same table as her castmates, sitting in the kitchen with the staff of the time; she was relegated to maid roles by white people and rejected by Black people, who did not understand her acceptance of the stereotype to which Hollywood had reduced her race.

timeline_list.title: Bugs Bunny
timeline_list.description: Amid a wave of classic short films, A Wild Hare (1940) is released, featuring the first appearance of Bugs Bunny.

timeline_list.title: The Great Dictator
timeline_list.description: The Great Dictator (1940) is a comic attack on Hitler. The film is banned in Germany, although Hitler confiscated a print and screened it twice.

timeline_list.title: Citizen Kane
timeline_list.description: Citizen Kane (1941) is released. Unable to prevent the film from being made, William Randolph Hearst tries to discredit it.

timeline_list.title: The Beginning of Film Noir
timeline_list.description: John Huston's (1906-1987) version of The Maltese Falcon (1941) is released. It is now recognized as the first distinctly noir film.

timeline_list.title: Hitchcock
timeline_list.description: Alfred Hitchcock's (1899-1980) first film noir is Shadow of a Doubt (1943).

timeline_list.title: The Beginning of Italian Neorealism
timeline_list.description: Considered one of the first Neorealist films, Ossessione (Obsession, 1943), directed by Luchino Visconti (1906-1976), falls into the clutches of Italy's Fascist censors, who destroy the film's negative. But Visconti saves a print.

timeline_list.title: The Revival of Swedish Cinema
timeline_list.description: In Sweden, Alf Sjöberg (1903-1980) directs Hets (Torment, 1944), from a screenplay by Ingmar Bergman (1918-2007); its international success sparks the revival of Swedish cinema.

timeline_list.title: Censorship Code in Japan
timeline_list.description: During the American occupation of Japan, a censorship code is created to impose liberal and democratic values on Japanese cinema.

timeline_list.title: The Emergence of the Term 'Noir'
timeline_list.description: Hollywood films are shown in Paris and called "noir". The Blue Dahlia (1946) and The Postman Always Rings Twice (1946) are released, as is The Big Sleep (1946).

timeline_list.title: Golden Years of American Cinema
timeline_list.description: Audiences pack American movie theaters like never before. The Best Years of Our Lives (1946) dominates the Oscars and the Golden Globes.

timeline_list.title: House Un-American Activities Committee
timeline_list.description: The House Un-American Activities Committee arrives in Los Angeles. Influential people in the industry condemn McCarthyism and the Hollywood blacklist.

timeline_list.title: Marilyn Monroe
timeline_list.description: Marilyn Monroe (1926-1962) makes her film debut in Dangerous Years (1947).

timeline_list.title: The End of the Golden Age
timeline_list.description: Vincente Minnelli (1903-1986) directs The Pirate (1948). That year would later be regarded as the last of Hollywood's Golden Age.

timeline_list.title: The Closest Thing to Neorealism
timeline_list.description: Luchino Visconti (1906-1976) directs La Terra Trema (1948). Its style comes close to what is now considered Neorealism.

timeline_list.title: The End of Classic Gangster Films
timeline_list.description: Raoul Walsh (1887-1980) directs White Heat (1949), which marks the end of the classic gangster films.

timeline_list.title: The Nationalization of Cinema in China
timeline_list.description: Junli Zheng (1911-1969) directs Wuya yu maque (Crows and Sparrows, 1949) in Shanghai. That same year, the dictator Mao nationalizes the Chinese film industry.

timeline_list.title: New Technologies
timeline_list.description: Hollywood introduces the world to widescreen and new tricks, such as 3D, to compete with a growing new medium: television.

timeline_list.title: Rashomon
timeline_list.description: Rashomon (1950), by Akira Kurosawa (1910-1998), presents four different versions of the story of a crime, in a format that would go on to be widely imitated in cinema.

timeline_list.title: Cold War Paranoia
timeline_list.description: The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) is the first of many science fiction films reflecting the fears stirred up by the Cold War.

timeline_list.title: Singin' in the Rain
timeline_list.description: Donen and Gene Kelly direct Singin' in the Rain (1952) for producer Arthur Freed's unit at MGM, at the height of the studio's creativity.

timeline_list.title: Ida Lupino
timeline_list.description: Actress Ida Lupino becomes the first woman to direct a film noir, The Hitch-Hiker (1953).

timeline_list.title: The Leather-Jacketed Rebel
timeline_list.description: The Wild One (1953) immortalizes Marlon Brando (1924-2004) as the leather-jacketed rebel.

timeline_list.title: Seven Samurai
timeline_list.description: Japan's Toho studio releases the first of the Godzilla monster movies. Akira Kurosawa (1910-1998) redefines the Western with Shichinin no Samurai (Seven Samurai, 1954).

timeline_list.title: Finnish Cinema
timeline_list.description: Ordet (1955), by Carl Dreyer (1889-1968), is probably the greatest Danish film of the 1950s. Tuntematon sotilas (The Unknown Soldier, 1955), by Edvin Laine (1905-1989), is released – the biggest hit in Finnish cinema.

timeline_list.title: James Dean
timeline_list.description: East of Eden (1955) and Rebel Without a Cause (1955) are released. James Dean (1931-1955) dies in a car crash at age 24, becoming immortalized on screen.

timeline_list.title: Elvis Presley
timeline_list.description: Elvis Presley (1935-1977) releases his first hit, "Heartbreak Hotel," and appears on national television for the first time.

timeline_list.title: References
timeline_list.description: Hollywood removes racial slurs from films and allows references to drugs, abortion, and prostitution.

timeline_list.title: Norwegian Cinema
timeline_list.description: Bergman directs Det sjunde inseglet (The Seventh Seal, 1957) and Smultronstället (Wild Strawberries, 1957). Ni Liv (Nine Lives, 1957), by Arne Skouen (1913-2003), draws international attention to Norwegian cinema.

timeline_list.title: French New Wave
timeline_list.description: Le Beau Serge (1958) is released and is considered the first film of the French New Wave movement.

timeline_list.title: The Great Epics
timeline_list.description: The Oscar record-holder Ben-Hur (1959) marks the apotheosis of epic films. Rawhide, starring Clint Eastwood (b. 1930), premieres on CBS.

timeline_list.title: Angry Young Men
timeline_list.description: Look Back in Anger (1959) is released. The film ushers in the era of the "angry young men" in British cinema.

timeline_list.title: The First Influences on James Bond
timeline_list.description: North by Northwest (1959), by Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980), is released, a landmark of the genre that influenced the early James Bond films.
